claim: Bansal et al. (2019) introduced the compatibility of an AI update with prior user experience and defined the compatibility score C(h1,h2) = sum_x A(x,h1(x))*A(x,h2(x)) / sum_x A(x,h1(x)): the fraction of examples on which the old model recommends the correct action where the updated model also does (1 if no new errors, 0 if all errors are new).
note: Definition (Compatibility Score), Eq. 1, p. 3 of the AAAI OJS PDF, checked on a rendered page image.

claim: Srivastava et al. (2020) named and defined backward trust compatibility BTC = sum_i 1[h1(x_i)=y_i, h2(x_i)=y_i] / sum_i 1[h1(x_i)=y_i] and backward error compatibility BEC = sum_i 1[h1(x_i)!=y_i, h2(x_i)!=y_i] / sum_i 1[h2(x_i)!=y_i]; they state that BTC matches Bansal et al.'s compatibility score.
note: Eqs. 1-2 of arXiv:2008.04572v1 checked on a rendered page image; reference [3] is Bansal et al. 2019. The KDD camera-ready was not compared with arXiv v1. Primary source for BTC/BEC: Srivastava 2020; for the underlying score: Bansal 2019.

claim: Yan et al. (2021) defined the negative flip rate NFR = (1/N) sum_i 1(yhat_i^new != y_i, yhat_i^old = y_i) and a relative NFR = NFR / ((1 - ER_old) * ER_new).
source_ids: cited anchor Yan et al. 2021 (re-read in T1-S020)
note: Eq. 2 and Eq. 11 of the CVF open-access version checked on rendered images. The denominator of relative NFR is the expected NFR if the two models erred independently.

claim: The negative flip impact NFI = NFR / ER_new was introduced by Cai et al. (2022), not by Yan et al. (2021).
source_ids: cited anchor Cai et al. 2022 (re-read in T1-S025); T1-P17
note: Cai et al. Section 3.1: 'we introduce the negative flip impact (NFI): NFI = NFR/ER_new'. Yan et al. define relative NFR instead. MUSCLE also attributes NFI to Cai et al.

claim: Prediction churn was defined by Milani Fard et al. (2016) as the expected fraction of examples on which two models' predictions differ: C(f1,f2) = E[1{f1(X) f2(X) < 0}] for binary classifiers with outputs in {-1,1}.
note: Eq. 1 of the NIPS 2016 paper; Section 1.2 defines churn as 'the expected percent of diffs'. Author order: official proceedings metadata lists Milani Fard first; the PDF title block shows Q. Cormier (ENS Lyon) above the Google authors. Cite as Milani Fard et al. per proceedings metadata.

claim: Shen et al. (2020) defined backward-compatible representations by an empirical criterion M(phi_new, phi_old; Q, D) > M(phi_old, phi_old; Q, D) and an update gain normalised by the best backfilled new model; 'backfilling' means re-processing every stored gallery item with the new model.
note: Eqs. 1, 2 and 9 of arXiv:2003.11942v3 checked on rendered images; backfilling defined in the abstract and Fig. 1 caption.

claim: Traeuble et al. (2021) formalised the Prediction Update Problem for stored predictions on unlabelled data, with 'Replace (a.k.a. backfilling)' as a baseline and NFR computed as the cumulative negative flips divided by N*T.
note: Sections 2 and 6.1 of the NeurIPS PDF. BTC/BEC formal definitions are in Appendix A.2, which was not read.

claim: All the classical update-compatibility metrics (compatibility score, BTC, BEC, NFR, relative NFR, NFI, churn, GBC, robust conditional-distribution compatibility) are defined for discrete predictions judged correct or incorrect (or equal or different), at a single timepoint.
source_ids: T1-P01; T1-P02; T1-P05; T1-P09; T1-P11; T1-P18; cited Yan 2021 and Cai 2022
note: Verified in full text for compatibility score, BTC, BEC, NFR, relative NFR, NFI and churn; GBC (Sakai 2022) and the robust metric (Matsuno and Sakuma 2023) checked only at abstract level, where both are described for classifiers.

claim: A compatibility metric for continuous model outputs already exists: Otles et al. (2023) define a threshold-free rank-based compatibility C^R for continuous risk scores, with a general form for ordered, including real-valued, labels.
note: Eq. 3 and Appendix Eq. 6 checked on rendered images (arXiv) and the same passages found in the PMLR PDF. A statement that no compatibility metric exists for continuous outputs would therefore be wrong.

claim: Echterhoff et al. (MUSCLE, 2024) extend compatibility metrics to continuous evaluation scores through the per-instance score difference D(x)=S(M_v2(x),y)-S(M_v1(x),y), with NFR~ and PFR~ (fractions of instances with D<0 and D>0) and mean regression and gain magnitudes m_r and m_g.
note: Section 3.2 of arXiv:2407.09435 checked on rendered images; the EMNLP Findings version was not compared line by line.

claim: Rank-based compatibility (C^R) is insensitive to a monotone calibration shift between versions, so it would not register the kind of between-version volume shift that produces the paper's retention cost.
note: Follows from Eq. 3/6, which depend only on orderings of the two models' outputs; Otles et al. state that rank concordance 'may be more robust to calibration shifts'. The application to volumes is our inference, not the authors' claim.

claim: No inspected source defines or evaluates a compatibility metric for a change measured between two timepoints by two model versions (mixed-version longitudinal change), in machine learning or medical imaging.
source_ids: All T1 papers; T1-S034 to T1-S094
note: Absence statement limited to the logged search (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar where reachable, arXiv, PubMed, Europe PMC, NeurIPS 2016-2025 titles, web search) up to 12 Oct 2026; it does not certify novelty. Closest: cross-version comparison of stored outputs in retrieval (Shen 2020; hot-refresh, Zhang 2022) and stored predictions (Traeuble 2021), none longitudinal or measurement-based.

claim: Retraining on the same data, or changing only the random seed, already produces incompatibility (negative flips or reduced BTC/BEC).
source_ids: T1-P02; T1-P09; cited Yan 2021; cited Cai 2022
note: Srivastava: 25 logistic-regression trials on identical FICO data gave BTC 94.5 +/- 1.31% and BEC 78.3 +/- 2.15%. Yan: two ResNet-152 runs with the same 78.3% accuracy differ on 10.4% of ImageNet validation samples. Xie: seed change alone gave up to 3.56% negative flips. Cai: at least 1.55% NFR from seed changes. Supports citing the paper's continued-training (same data) control as consistent with ML findings.

claim: The term and first formal treatment of update compatibility are attributed differently across papers: Traeuble et al. credit Bansal et al. (2019); Cai et al. say update regression was 'first studied' by Shen et al. (2020); prediction churn (Milani Fard et al. 2016) predates both.
source_ids: T1-P04; T1-P01; T1-P03; T1-P05; cited Cai 2022
note: Dates from registries: NIPS 2016 (churn), AAAI 2019 (published online 17 Jul 2019), CVPR 2020 (arXiv March 2020). The revision should not repeat the 'first studied by Shen' attribution.

claim: In continual learning, backward transfer BWT = (1/(T-1)) sum_{i<T} (R_T,i - R_i,i) (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato 2017) measures retained performance on earlier tasks, not agreement between model versions; medical segmentation continual-learning benchmarks report Dice-based BWT.
note: GEM Eq. 3; Lifelong nnU-Net reports Dice, BWT and FWT and no volume agreement.

claim: Individual-level instability of continuous predictions between models is quantified in clinical prediction modelling by the mean absolute prediction error between bootstrap and original model predictions (MAPE_i = sum_b |p_bi - p_i| / B).
note: Riley and Collins 2023, Section 3.2.3. In their simulation section MAPE is also used against true risks; the bootstrap definition is the model-to-model one.

claim: Distilling from the old (base) model is equivalent to training with an explicit predictive-churn constraint.
note: Stated in the abstract and introduction of Jiang et al.; the proof was not checked. Supports the rationale for the manuscript's distillation control.

claim: In ML systems, an update that corrects a previously mis-calibrated output can harm downstream consumers that adapted to the old calibration (undeclared consumers; CACE).
note: Sculley et al. 2015, Sections 2 and 3 ('a silent update that corrects the signal will have sudden ramifications for the model').

claim: Backward-compatible embedding systems treat 'keep every model version' (Keep-All), 'never update' (Fix-0) and learned backward transformations between versions as alternative strategies, judged by downstream task degradation.
note: Hu et al. 2022, Sections 1 and 3-4 of arXiv v1. Mapping these to the paper's strategies (one version per patient, no update, cross-calibration, reprocessing) is our analogy.

claim: Manuscript sentence (Introduction): 'These studies evaluate predictions at a single timepoint. None of those we inspected asks whether an update preserves a continuous measurement that is compared across two timepoints.'
note: Still accurate for all inspected sources, but incomplete: cross-version comparison of stored outputs is the core of backward-compatible representation learning (Shen 2020; hot-refresh upgrades) and of prediction updates (Traeuble 2021), and compatibility metrics for continuous outputs exist (Otles 2023; MUSCLE 2024). The revision should acknowledge these and narrow the claim to longitudinal measurement change.

claim: Manuscript bibliography entry yan2021 gives pages 14294-14303.
note: Crossref (IEEE) record for DOI 10.1109/CVPR46437.2021.01407 gives 14294-14303; the CVF open-access PDF is paginated 14299-14308. The manuscript's entry matches the DOI record.

claim: Manuscript Methods: backward-compatible weight interpolation theta_alpha = alpha*theta_old + (1-alpha)*theta_new, adapted from Schumann et al. (2024).
note: Schumann et al. Eq. 6: theta_BCWI = alpha*theta_old + (1-alpha)*theta_new; larger alpha moves closer to the old model. Note that in Schumann et al. the new model is fine-tuned from the old one (Eq. 5).

claim: Manuscript Introduction: Wang, Wu and Qin (2024) studied 'compatibility between old and updated models for incremental nuclei segmentation'.
note: Accurate as a description of a compatibility-inspired distillation loss for class-incremental segmentation; the paper defines no compatibility metric, so it should not be cited as a metric source.

claim: Wu et al. (2021): improving an upstream model can make downstream models worse even after they are retrained (self-defeating improvement).
note: Definition 2.1 and abstract of the NeurIPS 2021 paper.

claim: Hatherley and Sparrow (2023) distinguish diachronic evolution (change over time) from synchronic variation of adaptive ML systems and argue that a system differing from its previous iterations is hard for clinicians to trust.
note: Abstract and the section on challenges for physician judgement (open-access full text).

claim: Versions of clinical AI software can shift quantitative outputs while improving accuracy (VSBONE BSI values fell with each upgrade in metastasis-negative patients while AUC rose).
note: Abstract only; magnitude of the shift not checked. Overlaps T2.

claim: A deep-learning attenuation-correction model re-tuned for scanner software versions kept longitudinal amyloid PET SUVR repeatability (wCV, ICC) comparable to CT-based correction.
note: Abstract only; full text not retrievable. The upgrade concerned the scanner, and the network was fine-tuned per configuration; the study does not compare stored and reprocessed values (per abstract).

claim: Sakai (2022) showed that existing backward-compatibility metrics essentially assess the same quantity and proposed a generalised backward compatibility metric.
note: Abstract only (ACM DL blocked). Do not reproduce the GBC formula without reading the paper.

claim: Medical-imaging literature does not use the ML update-compatibility vocabulary (backward compatibility, negative flips, churn) for clinical model updates.
note: Europe PMC title/abstract search (2016-2026) returned 18 records, none applying these metrics to a clinical model update; the only medical update-consistency audit found (Zhang 2026, T1-P22) uses its own heatmap metric. Absence within this search only.

claim: Otles et al. (2023) describe C^R as the first rank-based compatibility measure.
note: Authors' own claim ('to the best of our knowledge'); S2 lists only one citing work, so no later extension was found.

claim: A vendor update of a commercial deep-learning auto-contouring product changed organ contours, including a loss of accuracy the vendor did not document.
note: AI-Rad Companion Organs RT VA30/VA50/VA60: brain contour handling changed, rectum HD worse (0.76 to 1.13 cm), bladder improved; authors state that the rectum change was not disclosed in the vendor's specifications or documentation. Contours only, not volumes; abstract misprints VA60 as VA50.

claim: A commercial treatment-planning-system upgrade that retrained auto-segmentation models on expanded data produced structure-specific regressions despite overall similar or better performance.
note: RayStation 11B to 2024A SP3: 8 OAR models retrained; left-lung DSC fell (p=0.03), spinal-cord DSC fell (p<0.001) with one failed contour; overall consistent. Reference is clinical contours.

claim: Successive versions of a commercial AI contouring product (six Limbus AI versions) improved retrained structures.
note: Abstract-level; breast DSC fell 1% between v1.5 and v1.8B3, not significant.

claim: Two versions of the same lung-nodule volumetry software gave different volumes (agreement in 2 of 100 nodules), and the authors recommend using the same version and algorithm for growth assessment.
note: Numbers and recommendation are in the abstract; full text not read. Mean variability 1.66% is relative; the 71% figure compares two algorithms within one version and must not be quoted as a version effect.

claim: An upgrade of a commercial perfusion-CT platform changed tumour perfusion parameters substantially (blood volume about 60% higher).
note: Relative differences of means: BF +20.4%, BV +59.5%, PS +106%, MTT -14.3%.

claim: QIBA requires the same software version at both timepoints for CT volume change.
note: Verified for the Small Lung Nodule profile (same Image Analysis Tool: manufacturer, model, version, at all time points). The CT Tumor Volume Change (CTV-AD) profile requires the same Image Analysis Tool and re-processing of the first timepoint if a different tool was used, but does not say 'version' explicitly. Phrase per profile.

claim: The QIBA CT tumour-volume-change profile requires the baseline to be re-processed when it was measured with a different analysis tool.
note: Sections 3.2 and A.9.2: 'Shall re-process the first timepoint if it was processed by a different Image Analysis Tool or Radiologist'; Appendix B repeats it.

claim: QIBA's FDG-PET/CT profile requires analysis software versions to be specified and used consistently across sequential lesion measurements, recorded, and supported for re-analysis with prior versions.
note: Sections 3.4.3 and 4.5 (Software version back-testing compatibility); same-scanner same-software-version recommendation in 3.6.4.

claim: FDA trial-imaging guidance warns that software upgrades during a trial can produce image changes misattributed to clinical change and asks charters to specify important software.
note: Appendix A, p. 12. The passage concerns software generally (mainly acquisition/processing); it does not require re-measuring baselines with a new analysis version.

claim: Oncology trial imaging guidance (charters, independent central review, RECIST working group) requires the same analysis-software version at baseline and follow-up.
note: No such explicit rule found in FDA 2018 guidance or in the screened central-review literature (Ford 2009 abstract). Only QIBA profiles (T2-P19 to P21) and the EHDN opinion (T2-P23, neuro) state version rules. Do not make this claim.

claim: After a commercial OCT segmentation update, combining stored old-version baselines with new-version follow-up changed estimated longitudinal atrophy, and the authors recommend re-segmenting baselines with the same version.
note: Accepted manuscript read: mixed -0.63 um vs old/old -0.95 um (difference 0.32 um, p<0.001) and new/new -0.71 um (0.08 um, p=0.136). AAM reports old/old vs new/new as 0.18 um although the means differ by 0.24 um; check the published version before quoting that number.

claim: A FreeSurfer version change can leave within-version reliability high while between-version agreement is poor for some structures.
note: Pallidum ICC 0.34 (v7.1 vs v5.3), 0.36 (v6.0 vs v5.3); cingulate thickness ICC 0.37-0.61 (v7.1 vs older); within-version reliability generally high.

claim: Commercial AI updates change output score scales, so thresholds calibrated on the previous version give different sensitivity and specificity.
note: CAD4TB v5/v6/v7: similar AUC, medians 28/35/11, threshold 40 sensitivity 79.8/88.9/66.7%. Lunit 3.1 to 3.9: old 90%-sensitivity threshold gave 96.4% sensitivity and 23.1% (vs 45.8%) specificity.

claim: A commercial mammography AI update that changed architecture and training data improved AUC but lowered the score of some cancers.
note: Transpara 1.7 to 2.1: AUC 0.908 to 0.928; 1.5% of screen-detected and 12.0% of interval cancers had lower scores. Do not quote the v1.7 AUC confidence interval, which is misprinted (0.986-0.920).

claim: An AI bone-age update left accuracy unchanged but shifted the reported standard-deviation scores.
note: BoneXpert v2 vs v3: MAE 0.89 vs 0.88 years; SDS 0.19 vs 0.56 (SDS units, not years).

claim: Vendors retrain commercial AI with additional data and release it under the same product name.
note: Codlin 2025 states it for TB CAD; Larsen 2026 reports vendor statements of new architecture and data; Barati 2026 documents retrained models in a TPS upgrade.

claim: Public segmentation models are retrained between versions and their developers warn that outputs can differ (TotalSegmentator).
note: Developer documentation: v2 retrained all models, segmentations 'slightly different from v1'; v2.5.0 doubled MR training subjects, 'results can be different from previous versions'. No peer-reviewed quantification of v1 vs v2 volume differences found.

claim: Small software-dependent differences in nodule measurements can change guideline-based management.
note: Three different commercial products (not versions); BTS-based management differed, Fleischner did not; hypothetical management.

claim: Instrument changes during follow-up add an offset to measured longitudinal change that can be modelled as a fixed effect.
note: MRI scanner and sequence changes in ADNI (e.g. -1.81%, -1.63% PBVC); scanner, not software.

claim: International societies (Fleischner, BTS) recommend the same volumetry software version at follow-up.
note: Stated by Guedes Pinto 2023 citing the Fleischner 2017 management guideline; Fleischner (Bankier 2017; MacMahon 2017) and BTS 2015 full texts were blocked (HTTP 403). Cite QIBA (T2-P20) instead.

claim: Cardiac strain software upgrades change serial measurements (relevant to cardio-oncology monitoring).
note: QLAB 9.0 to 10.2 bias 2.2% strain units (ICC 0.88). A cardio-oncology same-software rule was not verified (T2-S089).

claim: No inspected source evaluates the longitudinal change error of mixing a stored old-model-version baseline with an updated-version follow-up against reprocessing, for a deep-learning segmentation update in CT tumour volumetry.
note: Bounded statement: scope = PubMed, Europe PMC, arXiv, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Crossref (Aug-Oct 2026 sweep), web search and citation chasing, through 12 Oct 2026. Closest precedent is OCT (Coric 2018), which compared processing scenarios without a reference change. Not a certification of novelty.

claim: The manuscript's statement that longitudinal neuroimaging (only) already has a working rule against changing software version.
note: True for neuroimaging (Gronenschild 2012 re-read), but incomplete: QIBA CT volumetry and PET profiles and OCT (Coric 2018) state the same rule; the novelty sentence 'which neuroimaging already follows' should be broadened.

claim: Wang 2026 (cited) reports an update that replaced the network architecture (DeepLab V3 to nnU-Net V2).
note: Already-cited anchor re-read in PMC13525157: first-generation DeepLab V3 (2018) replaced by nnU-Net V2 in December 2024; matches the manuscript's wording.

claim: Gronenschild 2012 (cited) advises users not to update FreeSurfer, OS or workstation during an ongoing study without repeating the analysis.
note: Already-cited anchor re-read in PMC3365894: 'users are discouraged to update to a new major release ... without repeating the analysis'; matches the manuscript's paraphrase.

claim: JCGM 200:2012 (VIM, 3rd edition) is the current published International Vocabulary of Metrology (checked 2026-10-12).
note: BIPM JCGM publications page lists JCGM 200:2012 (DOI 10.59161/JCGM200-2012) as the VIM; JCGM-WG2 page shows VIM4 only as a 2nd committee draft (2023 documents). Re-check before submission.

claim: VIM 2.20 repeatability condition of measurement: 'condition of measurement, out of a set of conditions that includes the same measurement procedure, same operators, same measuring system, same operating conditions and same location, and replicate measurements on the same or similar objects over a short period of time'.
note: JCGM 200:2012 p.23. Line-break hyphens removed when transcribing.

claim: VIM 2.21 measurement repeatability: 'measurement precision under a set of repeatability conditions of measurement'.

VIM 2.24 reproducibility condition of measurement: 'condition of measurement, out of a set of conditions that includes different locations, operators, measuring systems, and replicate measurements on the same or similar objects'; NOTE 1 'The different measuring systems may use different measurement procedures.'
note: p.24. Note 2: a specification should give the conditions changed and unchanged.

claim: VIM 2.25 measurement reproducibility: 'measurement precision under reproducibility conditions of measurement'.

VIM 2.22 intermediate precision condition: same measurement procedure, same location, replicate measurements over an extended period of time, 'but may include other conditions involving changes'; NOTE 1 'The changes can include new calibrations, calibrators, operators, and measuring systems.'
note: p.24. A within-site model update over time arguably fits this condition better than 2.24 (interpretation).

claim: VIM 2.6 measurement procedure: 'detailed description of a measurement according to one or more measurement principles and to a given measurement method, based on a measurement model and including any calculation to obtain a measurement result'.
note: p.18. That a trained model's inference is part of the 'calculation to obtain a measurement result' is an interpretation, not stated by VIM.

claim: VIM 2.39 calibration: 'operation that, under specified conditions, in a first step, establishes a relation between the quantity values with measurement uncertainties provided by measurement standards and corresponding indications with associated measurement uncertainties and, in a second step, uses this information to establish a relation for obtaining a measurement result from an indication'; NOTE 1 'In some cases, it may consist of an additive or multiplicative correction of the indication with associated measurement uncertainty.'
note: p.28. VIM calibration is against measurement standards; mapping an old version onto a new one is better called cross-calibration (ISCD usage), a term VIM does not define.

claim: VIM 2.47 metrological compatibility of measurement results: 'property of a set of measurement results for a specified measurand, such that the absolute value of the difference of any pair of measured quantity values from two different measurement results is smaller than some chosen multiple of the standard measurement uncertainty of that difference'.
note: p.32. NOTE 1: it replaces 'staying within the error' and is the criterion for deciding whether two results refer to the same measurand. NOTE 2: correlation between measurements affects the standard uncertainty of the difference (lower for positive covariance).

claim: VIM 2.46 metrological comparability: 'comparability of measurement results, for quantities of a given kind, that are metrologically traceable to the same reference'.
note: p.31. Comparability (common reference) differs from compatibility (agreement within uncertainty).

claim: QIBA terminology (Kessler et al. 2015): the 95% precision limit is 2.77 x wSD; it is called the repeatability coefficient (RC) when the wSD is obtained under repeatability conditions and the reproducibility coefficient (RDC) when obtained under reproducibility conditions.
note: Kessler OnlineFirst p.10 (verbatim: 'If s corresponds to the wSD under repeatability conditions, the value 2.77s is sometimes called the RC and it is called a RDC if s corresponds to the wSD under reproducibility conditions'). Raunig 2015 and Obuchowski 2015 define RC and RDC as least significant differences under identical vs different conditions.

claim: Kessler et al. state that reproducibility 'still requires the same measurement procedure, the same operating conditions, and a short period of time between measurements. It is only location, operator, and/or measuring system that may differ.'
note: Quote verified (OnlineFirst p.10). It is narrower than VIM 2.24 Note 1; cite VIM for the definition and Kessler for QIB usage.

claim: Reproducibility variance is the repeatability variance plus between-condition variance (sigma^2_reproducibility = sigma^2_repeatability + sigma^2_between-factors), and RDC = 2.77 sqrt(sigma^2_condition + sigma^2_case-by-condition + sigma^2_error), where the condition may be an algorithm.
note: Raunig 2015 eq. (15) and RDC section; Obuchowski 2015 section 7.2. Read in NIH author manuscripts.

claim: For log-normally distributed volumes, wCV = sqrt(exp(sigma^2_ln) - 1), approximately sigma_ln, so limits on the log scale back-transform to asymmetric percentage limits exp(+/-RC_ln) - 1.
note: Raunig eqs (11)-(13); Obuchowski 2018 eqs (8)-(10); Bland-Altman 1986 on antilogged limits as ratios.

claim: Sullivan et al. (Radiology 2015) state that if the same subject is measured at t1 and t2 by different operators, both within- and between-operator variance components determine what measured change can be interpreted as true change.
note: Section 'Measuring Biological Change' (PMC HTML). Their example is operators; extending it to model versions is an analogy.

claim: Obuchowski et al. (2015, already cited) note that test-retest studies omit 'possible change in imaging device (model or software) between images' and that 'software or hardware upgrades may introduce more bias and/or less precision in the derived QIB'.
note: Author manuscript PMC4263694, sections 2 and 9. Already in the manuscript's reference list (obuchowski2015).

claim: A 95% interval for true change when the two timepoints are measured under different fixed conditions can be formed as (d - delta_hat) +/- 1.96 sqrt(V_d + V_delta_hat), where delta_hat is the estimated fixed condition effect (reproducibility interval approach).
note: Obuchowski et al. 2015 (SMMR 24:107-140) section 4.5.2, illustrated for slice thickness 0.8 vs 5 mm in QIBA 3A data, not for software versions.

claim: QIBA CTV-AD (2022) Change Detection Claim: a true change in lung tumour volume has occurred with 95% confidence if the measured change is larger than 24%, 29% or 39% for longest in-plane diameter 50-100, 35-49 or 10-34 mm; Repeatability Claim wCV 0.085, 0.103, 0.141.
note: Section 1.2, p.3. 2.77 x wCV gives 23.5%, 28.5%, 39.1%. Claims are lung-only and described as a hypothesis based on committee assessment.

claim: The QIBA CTV-AD profile requires the same image analysis tool (and radiologist) at both timepoints and requires the baseline to be re-processed if it was processed by a different tool or radiologist.
note: A.9.1 p.29: 'The Profile requires that the same Image Analysis Tool and the same Radiologist measure both timepoints of a given tumor.' A.9.2/3.5 (pp.9, 29): 'Shall re-process the first timepoint if it was processed by a different Image Analysis Tool or Radiologist.' App. B p.30: 'the current radiologist and image analysis tool must repeat the baseline measurement for the result to be conformant'. Tool checklist (p.6): 'Shall be able to re-process the first timepoint'.

claim: The QIBA CTV-AD profile explicitly requires the same software VERSION at both timepoints.
note: Not stated. The profile says 'same Image Analysis Tool'; the tool checklist records 'Make/Model/Version'; 'same manufacturer, model and version' appears only for scanners and is 'strongly encouraged' (A.6.1, p.25). Whether a new version counts as a 'different Image Analysis Tool' is not defined. The explicit version rule is in the small-nodule profile (T3-C22).

claim: QIBA CTV-AD Table B-1 (informative): with the same scanner and radiologist, the minimum detectable volume change is 8% vs 37% (>50 mm), 14% vs 60% (35-49 mm) and 28% vs 75% (10-34 mm) for the same vs a different analysis tool; with different radiologists and tools on the same scanner it is 136% for 10-34 mm.
note: Checked against the rendered table (pp.30-31). Values are informative, 'not Claims', computed as 1.96 x sqrt(2 x wCV^2) with additive variance components ('an assumption that has not yet been tested'). 'Different analysis tool' means a different product, not a version.

claim: The QIBA small lung nodule profile (2023) requires the same image analysis tool (manufacturer, model, version) at all timepoints.
note: Section 3.10.1 p.28: 'different versions of the same program or its components may change its performance, a nodule being evaluated for change must be analyzed at both time points with the same software program (manufacturer, model, and version)'; 3.10.2 p.29: 'Shall use the same Image Analysis Tool (manufacturer, model, version) for measurements at all time points.'

claim: QIBA small-nodule CVs: 0.29, 0.23, 0.19, 0.16, 0.14 for 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 mm nodules (minimum detectable difference 80.3% to 38.8%).
note: Table 1 p.7, checked visually. Solid lung nodules in low-dose screening only.

claim: Same-day repeat CT (within 15 min) of NSCLC tumours: computer-aided volumetric 95% limits of agreement -12.1% to +13.4% (32 patients).
note: Matches the manuscript's 'about -12% to +13%' (zhao2009). The limits are for the computer-aided method, not radiologists' manual measurements.

claim: Oxnard et al. (2011) provide a volume repeatability benchmark.
note: Oxnard measured diameters only (-23% to +31%; 84% within +/-10%). It is a diameter benchmark for response-category context, not a volume benchmark.

claim: On RIDER coffee-break scans, semi-automated volume percent change was 23.4 +/- 105% (mean +/- SD) with independent reads and 7.4 +/- 44.2% with locked sequential reads.
note: Tables 1-2, pooled over 5 readers x 32 lesions. Mean +/- SD of percent change, not an RC.

claim: In the QIBA 3A phantom challenge, RC was 9.0% when one algorithm measured a nodule twice, versus an RDC of 22.1% of average volume when different algorithms were used (QIBA-compliant nodules).
note: Results and Table 7 (RDC 1307.39 mm3 = 22.12% of average volume; wCV 3.25%). Phantom nodules; vendors' algorithms, not versions.

claim: On clinical coffee-break data, change could be measured to within +/-14% with any of nine algorithms (same algorithm at both timepoints), whereas inter-algorithm reproducibility was 58-84%.
note: Buckler 2015 (already cited) abstract and results; tumours >10 mm for the +/-14% statement.

claim: Small-lesion repeat-scan benchmarks: 95% limits of interscan volume difference -21.2% to +23.8% (218 nodules of 16-473 mm3) and -20.4% to +21.9% (151 nodules; -19.3% to +20.4% below 10 mm).
note: Numbers verified in abstracts only (Gietema 2007; Wormanns 2004); lung metastases, one commercial package each; full texts not read.

claim: Repeat-scan precision of small-nodule volume depends on the algorithm (median per-nodule CV 4.6% vs 8.7%).
note: Jirapatnakul 2024 abstract; 4-6 repeat scans in one session.

claim: Repeatability or test-retest data for CT volumetry of liver metastases, pancreatic tumours or melanoma metastases exist.
note: No scan-rescan volumetry study was found for these sites within the searched scope (PubMed T3-S032 to T3-S034, Europe PMC T3-S088). Only inter-/intra-observer or inter-method data: liver metastases incl. pancreatic-cancer metastases (Rothe 2013), lung/liver/lymph-node metastases (Wulff 2012), pancreatic GTV delineation (Versteijne 2017). Obuchowski 2015 notes contrast timing makes liver coffee-break studies impractical.

claim: Bone densitometry practice: without cross-calibration, no quantitative comparison with the prior machine can be made and a new baseline should be established.
note: ISCD Official Positions 2023 (web): 'If a cross-calibration assessment is not performed, no quantitative comparison to the prior machine can be made. Consequently, a new baseline BMD and intra-system LSC should be established.' Hardware/system changes, not software versions.

claim: A densitometry analysis-software upgrade changed femoral neck BMD (95% LoA -0.057 to 0.063 g/cm2) and the authors recommended reanalysing earlier scans with the new software for longitudinal assessment.
note: Wong & Griffiths 2002 abstract only. Overlaps T2 (software version dependence).

claim: Clinical laboratories verify each new reagent lot against the current lot with patient samples and predefined acceptance limits (CLSI EP26, 2nd ed., 2022), and verify comparability of patient results across instruments within a health system (CLSI EP31, 2nd ed., 2025).
note: Titles, editions, dates and scope verified on CLSI product pages; guideline text not read (paywalled).

claim: Lot-verification protocols that compare each new lot only with its predecessor do not detect cumulative shifts across lots.
note: Thompson & Chesher 2018 abstract. Laboratory analogy for successive model updates.

claim: The coefficient of individual agreement without a reference is psi = [MSD(Y1,Y1') + MSD(Y2,Y2')] / [2 MSD(Y1,Y2)], and agreement is considered acceptable if psi > 0.8.
note: Haber, Gao & Barnhart 2010 eq. (1); the 0.8 threshold is the authors' suggestion citing Barnhart 2007 and Haber & Barnhart 2008 (abstract level).

claim: Using the same segmentation software at all timepoints of a longitudinal study is recommended in the CT volumetry literature.
note: Kalpathy-Cramer 2016 abstract states the recommendation; QIBA profiles require it (tool for CTV-AD; tool and version for small nodules).

claim: No inspected source defines a compatibility metric for an update of a trained segmentation (or other analysis-software) version evaluated on longitudinal change error, or compares stored old-version baselines with reprocessing.
note: Absence statement limited to the logged scope (PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar contexts of Kessler 2015/Zhao 2009/Obuchowski 2015, QIBA wiki, BIPM, ISCD, CLSI; 2026-10-12). Closest: ISCD inter-system LSC after cross-calibration (hardware), QIBA Table B-1 (different tool, informative), reproducibility interval with a fixed condition effect (slice thickness), RC vs RDC across algorithms, Wong & Griffiths 2002 (reanalysis after upgrade, no metric). Novelty is not certified.

claim: 'Metrological compatibility' (VIM 2.47) has been applied to medical-image measurements.
note: Europe PMC phrase search (T3-S048) returned 3 non-imaging records; no imaging use found in the searched scope.

claim: Change in lesion size is a different measurand from absolute size, so characterizing single-timepoint performance does not characterize change.
note: Obuchowski 2015 section 2: 'Each of these has a different measurand and associated uncertainty; characterizing one type does not mean that other types are characterized.' Supports the manuscript's point that overlap gains do not certify compatibility.

claim: Between-observer differences in manual RECIST measurements can exceed the 20% progression threshold (pooled 95% limits of agreement about -22% to +25% for single-lesion diameters and -31% to +30% for the interval change of a single lesion).
note: Numbers match the abstract of a 12-study meta-analysis; they are limits of agreement of relative measurement differences, not category-change rates; full text not read.

claim: When readers select the same target lesions they agree on progression in about 98% of patients; with different lesions in about 55%.
note: 97.7% vs 55.3% agreement on progression (PD vs non-PD) by target-selection subgroup; 316 patients, three readers; not an overall rate.

claim: Re-imaging within minutes moves about 3% of lesion measurements across the RECIST progression threshold without any true change.
note: 3% of 90 lesion-reader pairs (30 NSCLC lesions, three radiologists, side-by-side unidimensional); none met partial response; per lesion-reader pair, not per patient; read via tool extraction of the PMC page and checked against the abstract.

claim: Between observers, the probability of misclassifying a single lesion's progression is about 30% (unidimensional); within one observer the probability of misclassifying response is about 3%.
note: Numbers verified in the abstract (43%/30% bidimensional/unidimensional progression between observers; 2.5%/3.0% response within observer); modelled probabilities per tumour on printed film; computation method not read (full text 403).

claim: Measurement variability alone changes the patient-level RECIST 1.1 category in about 6% (same observer) to 12% (different observers) of cases.
note: 6.3% and 12% relative to the mean result of four observers (not pairwise); 20 patients; target lesions only.

claim: Changing the measurement method (manual to automated, or diameter to volume) changes the patient-level category in 15-27% of patients, and semi-automatic tools do not remove between-observer category discordance.
note: Keil 2014: 11/41 (27%) manual vs automated and 6/41 (15%) unidimensional vs volumetric, one breast-cancer cohort; van Kessel 2012: between-observer discordance 17.8% manual, 22.2% automatic diameter and volume. Abstract-level; generalisation beyond these cohorts not shown.

claim: Investigator and central review disagree on progression in about 18% of trial patients overall and about 12% in melanoma.
note: 17.7% (n = 20,908) and 11.8%; 39 pembrolizumab trials; whole RECIST including lesion selection, non-target and new lesions; up to 10 target lesions allowed.

claim: Independent double reads in central review disagree on whether progression occurred in about one in five patients.
note: 21.0% PD-declared discrepancy across five lung trials (1724 patients, 17 radiologists).

claim: The RECIST 1.1 thresholds of -30% and +20% in diameter correspond to -65.7% and +72.8% in volume for a sphere, and -65%/+73% volume equivalents have been applied to per-patient sums of lesion volumes.
note: Arithmetic 0.7^3 = 0.343 and 1.2^3 = 1.728; Prasad 2002 (abstract) and Zimmermann 2021 PJR (full text) applied them to summed volumes; Gong 2023, Vogel 2012 and Dahm 2024 also used -65%/+73%. RECIST 1.1 itself (Eisenhauer 2009, already cited) is the source of the diameter thresholds.

claim: RECIST 1.0 (Therasse et al. 2000) tabulated the volume equivalents -65%/+73%.
note: Only a secondary attribution (Zimmermann 2021 cites Therasse 2000 for the volumetric thresholds); the primary text is paywalled. Cite the sphere arithmetic or Prasad 2002 unless the authors check Therasse 2000 themselves.

claim: In liver metastases, a 20% diameter increase corresponds empirically to about a 65% volume increase, lower than the sphere value of 73%.
note: -65.3% and +64.6% from loess regression in colorectal liver metastases (348 patients, 4773 value pairs); proposed +/-65%.

claim: Lesion-level categories from RECIST-equivalent volume thresholds disagree with diameter-based RECIST categories in about 14% of lesion interpretations.
note: 13.9% of 2390 interpretations (478 lesions, three readers, two semi-automated tools); 6.6% substantive and 7.3% attributed to volumetric sensitivity; per interpretation, not per patient.

claim: Volume-based and diameter-based RECIST assign different patient-level categories in roughly 10-30% of patients.
note: Dahm 7/58 (12%), Vogel 6/58 (10%), Keil 6/41 (15%), Rothe 10-21%, Prasad 12/38 (32%), Zimmermann 12-34% per reader in an enriched sample. The range depends on cohort, thresholds and case mix; quote individual studies with conditions rather than one figure.

claim: Treating lesions as spheres overcalls progression compared with measured volumes.
note: Week 9: PD in 52 (sphere model) vs 31 (measured volume) of 593 patients; 25/52 (48%) sphere-model PD were SD by measured volume; kappa 0.63; renal cell carcinoma. Abstract P value (< .001) differs from the results (.017 and .053); cite counts.

claim: Volumetric response predicts outcome better than RECIST diameter response.
note: Positive in colorectal liver metastases (Wesdorp 2021 RFS in 118 resected patients; Abbas 2026 liver-only subgroup n = 43), null in Lubner 2017 (105 patients). Write 'some studies report', not 'established'.

claim: Mozley et al. (2012) supports volumetric thresholds of -65%/+73%.
note: Mozley used variability-derived volume cut-offs of about +/-25% in 10 patients and seven teams; cite it for reproducibility and sensitivity of volumes, not for -65%/+73%.

claim: Automated nnU-Net-based RECIST measurements in melanoma follow-up CT agree with radiologists about as well as radiologists agree with each other.
note: Cohen kappa 0.67-0.76 (automated vs mean manual) vs Fleiss kappa 0.68-0.79 among three readers; 58 patients, preselected target lesions.

claim: AI assistance raised patient-level RECIST target-lesion outcome agreement by 7.7 percentage points (72.5% to 80.4%).
note: Reported in percentage points in the paper's table; 212 patients, 23 readers, baseline lesions premeasured; exact agreement definition is in Appendix C (not read).

claim: Follow-up segmentation errors of a prompt-assisted longitudinal model changed the patient-level RECIST target-lesion category in about one in six melanoma patients.
note: 16.7% (43/258; Wilson 95% CI 12.6-21.7) on the same Longitudinal-CT data with an expert baseline; preprint version 1 (10 August 2026), not peer reviewed.

claim: Evidence on AI that assigns RECIST categories directly is sparse.
note: Four eligible studies (two image-based) in a PRISMA review searched to 6 December 2025.

claim: No published study has measured how a software or model version change alters response categories, or compared stored old-version baselines with reprocessed baselines for response assessment.
note: Absence statement only: PubMed (title/abstract), Europe PMC (including full text of open-access papers), OpenAlex search and forward/backward chasing from the anchors to 12 October 2026 found none; Semantic Scholar failed (HTTP 429). Write 'no inspected source', with this scope.

claim: Regulatory guidance warns that software changes during a trial can be misattributed to clinical change.
note: FDA 2018 says so for image-generation software upgrades and asks for software specification, version control where needed and QC of critical software functions; it does not mention segmentation-model versions.

claim: A RECIST-defined progression usually ends the current line of therapy, so a false progression call can stop an effective treatment.
note: Stated by Gong 2023 ('commonly results in the cessation of therapy') and the iRECIST guideline (two-sided cost of early discontinuation vs delayed salvage therapy); Siegel 2023 and Hodi 2016 describe potential premature removal or cessation. Authors' statements, not measured rates.

claim: Erroneous target-lesion measurements are the main cause of false progression calls in routine clinical reads.
note: 58% (61/105) of routine-read PD over-calls; single institution; 105 of 327 patients with PD on at least one read.

claim: A response misclassification rate of about 17% can cut the power of an 80%-powered trial to roughly 40-64% depending on the endpoint.
note: In silico: ORR 39%, DCR 54%, PFS 64%, OS 64%; based on pleural mesothelioma (mRECIST) discordance of 35%.

claim: Random tumour-measurement variability attenuates PFS hazard ratios towards 1.
note: Simulation; non-directional error; a systematic version bias is not modelled.

claim: In advanced melanoma on pembrolizumab, about 14% of patients were progressive by RECIST 1.1 but not by immune-related criteria, with intermediate survival.
note: 84/592 patients surviving >=12 weeks; 2-year OS 37.5% vs 77.6% and 17.3%.

claim: Lesion-level response categories often differ from the patient-level category.
note: 27.6% of target lesions did not follow their patient's category (MRI, liver); different target sets gave different PD calls in 34% of 200 patients (CT).

claim: In pancreatic adenocarcinoma, inter-reader agreement on RECIST response is low without registration support.
note: Kappa 0.23 for all readers (0.0 junior, 0.37 senior), 0.81 with registration; 30 neoadjuvant patients, primary tumours.

claim: Volume-change thresholds derived from measurement variability are much smaller than RECIST-equivalent volume thresholds.
note: QIBA +/-24, 29 or 39% by baseline size; +/-30% (Zhao 2014); +/-38% (Vogel 2012); about +/-25% (Mozley 2012); versus -65%/+73%.

claim: TotalSegmentator v2 retrained all models with more training images (1139 to 1559) and corrected label errors, and its documentation states that v2 segmentations differ slightly from v1 because all models were retrained.
note: resources/improvements_in_v2.md (accessed 2026-10-12): 'We increased the number of training images from 1139 to 1559' and 'The resulting segmentations will also be slightly different from v1, because all models have been retrained.' Weights tags agree (Task25x_..._1139subj for v1.5.6; Dataset29x_..._1559subj for v2.0.0). Size of the difference is not quantified anywhere inspected.

claim: The TotalSegmentator developer describes v2 as the same method as v1 with more data and classes.
note: Issue #179, comment by wasserth, 2023-09-30: 'the methods are just identical to v1. We just added more data and classes. So basically the v1 paper also applies for v2.' Also true per CHANGELOG 2.0.0: models were retrained with nnU-Net v2 instead of the customised nnU-Net v1, so the framework version changed too. Developer statement, not peer reviewed.

claim: Minor TotalSegmentator releases changed inference and post-processing defaults and replaced individual task models.
note: CHANGELOG: 2.1.0 total task step_size 0.5 to 0.8 ('only decreasing dice by 0.001'); 2.2.1 'major bugfix: rib labels were in wrong order'; 2.5.0 MR models retrained with double data ('results can be different from previous versions'); 2.8.0 and 2.9.0 resampling bug fixes; 2.12.0 heart-chamber post-processing; 2.13.0 coronary_arteries and lung_vessels models replaced, previous versions kept as _LEGACY; 2.16.0 default input resampling order 3 to 1 ('very similar segmentation accuracy').

claim: TotalSegmentator v3.0.0 weights (7 September 2026) were trained on 1830 subjects for the organ, cardiac and muscle parts.
note: Inferred from asset file names (Dataset831_TotalSegmentator_part1_organs_1830subj.zip etc.; vertebrae and ribs 1559subj). No release notes; v3.0.0 not on PyPI on 2026-10-12. Cite as 'asset names indicate' or omit.

claim: TotalSegmentator can write a run manifest that records software and model versions.
note: CHANGELOG 2.15.0 and README: '--report' writes 'a machine-readable JSON run manifest (software and model versions, resolved device, task, classes, runtime and the list of output files)'.

claim: Swapping between two nnU-Net-based whole-body CT segmenters changed organ volumes: within 10% for 19 of 33 organs in at least 80% of 315 patients, but by 20% or more in at least 20% of patients for adrenal glands, bladder, portal/splenic veins and thyroid; volumes differed significantly for 28 of 33 structures.
note: MOOSE v3.0.14 vs TotalSegmentator v2.0.5. Abstract and Results say 'less than 10%'; one Discussion sentence says 'less than 20%' for the same 19/33 organs (internal inconsistency); use the Results wording. 48%, 34%, 16%, 15% are the largest relative differences (bladder, veins, thyroid, adrenals). Organs, not lesions; cross-sectional.

claim: Three pancreas segmenters agreed poorly on pancreatic volume (ICC 0.50) although attenuation measures agreed (ICC 0.93 or more).
note: ICC two-way random, single measures, across TotalSegmentator, nnU-Net (MSD Task07) and DM-UNet; 9772 patients; volume ICC 0.50 (0.48-0.51), non-contrast 0.55, contrast 0.37. Overall three-algorithm ICC, not pairwise.

claim: With the framework held fixed, training data changed measurement reproducibility: an nnU-Net trained on 30 BTCV CTs had larger cross-phase volume deviation than TotalSegmentator (AVD 10.03% vs 6.50%).
note: AVD = absolute volume deviation between contrast phases of the same examination (reproducibility), not agreement between the two models. TotalSegmentator version not stated.

claim: Models differ in anatomical definitions and volumes, including between TotalSegmentator 1.5 and 2.6.
note: TotalSegmentator 1.5 segments heart substructures, 2.6 a single heart label; consensus-to-model volume ratios 60-85% (heart, 4 models), 45-90% (ribs), 0-95% (vertebrae). 18 series from 4 NLST patients, no ground truth; descriptive only. Numbers read in arXiv v2.

claim: Changing the click location within a lesion changes the output of a click-prompted CT lesion segmenter.
note: ULS23 baseline consistency Dice 0.787 +/- 0.252 across click locations; authors call this the model's 'intra-observer variability'. Dice, not volume; published MedIA version not read.

claim: In ULS23, a residual-encoder nnU-Net configuration outperformed the default nnU-Net on the test set (Dice 0.700 vs 0.651).
note: Table 2 row labels are offset in the extracted text; values matched to the text stating that the semi-supervised ResEnc baseline scored 0.703. Architecture-configuration effect on Dice only.

claim: A promptable CT tumour model's accuracy depended on the prompt mode: mean Dice 0.70 with a point or box and 0.79 after four simulated edits; long-axis median error 14.1% vs 9.6%.
note: Held-out ULS23/DeepLesion test set; external cohort 0.68/0.70/0.79. Pre-trained version (ONCOPILOT-zero) 0.58 externally. Error is the long-axis diameter, not volume.

claim: 3D promptable models follow imprecise mask prompts: nnInteractive over- or under-segments with dilated or eroded mask prompts.
note: Qualitative statement plus Dice trends on BTCV organs; SAM-Med3D robust to spatial shifts for most organs. No mL; ISBI 2026 acceptance per authors' arXiv comment, proceedings not checked.

claim: Prompt number and placement change SAM lesion segmentation substantially (ovarian tumours Dice 0.272 with one point vs 0.806 with five or more).
note: Abstract only; Dice not volume.

claim: Across six prompt types, promptable models differed (median DSC 0.75 nnInteractive, 0.70 MedSAM2, 0.54 SAM2) and richer prompts reduced variance.
note: Abstract only (IOP full text blocked by captcha); MRI GTVs; Dice not volume.

claim: Both the foundation-model architecture and the prompting strategy significantly affect head and neck tumour segmentation; enlarged boxes degrade SAM, MedSAM and nnInteractive.
note: Abstract only; repeated-measures ANOVA; Dice not volume.

claim: With training data held fixed, changing the architecture (MD-GRU vs nnU-Net) left cross-sectional bias and precision similar but changed longitudinal sensitivity (198 vs 161 patients per arm for a 30% effect).
note: Brain MRI WMH; each architecture measured both timepoints (no mixing); reference masks built by STAPLE from all five algorithms, so bias is relative to a consensus; 88% vs 92% of patients with positive 2-year change.

claim: A version update of a commercial brain volumetry tool improved overlap (hippocampal DSC 0.910 vs 0.892) and diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.977 vs 0.921).
note: Vendor-affiliated authors; between-version volume agreement not reported in this paper.

claim: After that update, volumes differed between versions (MRAE above 5% for half the measures) and the developers did not recommend mixing versions.
note: Conference abstract (Alzheimer's & Dementia 19(S3) e062107): 'The two versions of AccuBrain are not suggested for a mixed use.' Cross-sectional MRAE and ICC, no longitudinal change error. Pair with T5-C18; overlaps with part T2.

claim: Five architectures trained on the same data reached similar volume accuracy for vestibular schwannomas.
note: Abstract reports median RVE 0.07-0.08 for the top three models under the label 'RVE (%)'; whether this is 0.07% or 7% cannot be resolved without the full text (AJNR, not accessible). Do not cite the number.

claim: Foundation and promptable segmentation models are re-released with new weights or architectures: MedSAM to LiteMedSAM to MedSAM2; SAM-Med3D to SAM-Med3D-turbo; BiomedParse v1 to v2 (BoltzFormer architecture); VISTA3D bundles 0.4.1 to 0.5.13; nnInteractive checkpoint v1.0 with software 1.1.0 to 2.5.0.
note: Repository READMEs and the MONAI bundle changelog accessed 2026-10-12; documentation can change. VISTA3D bundle changes include 'use 0.3 overlap for inference' (0.4.8) and 'change sw padding mode to replicate' (0.5.7).

claim: Some developers recommend the newest model version by default.
note: BiomedParse README: 'We recommend using the latest version of the model.' nnInteractive README: the default model id resolves to the recommended model ('Don't hard-code a version here, so you automatically track whatever is currently recommended'); a version can be pinned.

claim: A peer-reviewed update of TotalSegmentator's cardiovascular structures was evaluated by overlap metrics (Dice, NSD), which improved for 5 of 6 enhanced structures.
note: Abstract only (not open access); no volume-shift analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Two runs of the same TotalSegmentator version on the same series need not produce identical masks.
note: Issue #445 (v1.5.6): developer attributes it to PyTorch/CUDA non-determinism and calls the variability 'minimal'; not quantified.

claim: Errors of a prompt-assisted longitudinal model at follow-up (with an expert baseline) changed RECIST target-lesion response in about one in six patients.
note: Research Square preprint (not peer reviewed); 43/258 (16.7%; 95% CI 12.6-21.7). Expert baseline, not an older model version. Overlaps with part T4.

claim: The published TotalSegmentator description (Radiology: AI 2023) refers to v1: 1204 CTs, nnU-Net, Dice 0.943.
note: README: 'Our Radiology AI publication refers to TotalSegmentator v1.'

claim: Between-algorithm reproducibility of CT tumour volume was much poorer than within-algorithm repeatability for the best algorithms (inter-algorithm 58-84% vs intra-algorithm 13-100%).
source_ids: buckler2015 (already cited by the manuscript; abstract read under T5-S064)
note: Semi-automated, pre-deep-learning algorithms on clinical thoracic CT test-retest data; 58% is for the four best-performing groups, 84% with all but the least performer. Already in the reference list, so reuse rather than add.

claim: TotalSegmentator Fast and Normal modes gave similar longitudinal variability (detrended within-participant CV 2.26-9.32%).
note: Abstract only; one mode per participant; version not given in the abstract.

claim: No inspected source measured the change error that arises when a baseline measured by one version of a foundation, promptable or public CT segmentation model is compared with a follow-up measured by another version.
source_ids: all T5 sources; scope in NOTES.md section 4
note: Absence statement bounded by 83 logged queries on 2026-10-12 (PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, Crossref, GitHub, web search). Closest: T5-P27 (cross-sectional between-version agreement), T5-P17 and T5-P24 (single-pipeline longitudinal measurement), T5-P29 (expert baseline vs model follow-up). Write as 'no inspected source'.

claim: AAPM TG-53 treats a new release of planning software as requiring acceptance/commissioning-type testing before clinical use, chosen from the vendor's release information, and lists vendor duties for version updates.
note: Content verified in the JASTRO translation: Ch. 5 opening paragraph, Table 5-1 'Variable' row, Appendix 1 A1.1.4, A1.2.5 and Table A1-2. The English wording was not seen; check Med Phys 25:1773-1829 before quoting.

claim: TG-53 recommends re-running benchmark tests after a planning-system upgrade.
note: TG-53 does not prescribe specific tests. It says new versions need acceptance and commissioning-type testing prioritised from vendor information, and periodic QA uses commissioning tests. 'Benchmark tests' appear in the acceptance-testing chapter. Safer: 'TG-53 requires that each new software version be tested before clinical release, with the tests chosen from the vendor's documentation of changes.'

claim: AAPM MPPG 5.b recommends repeating a subset of commissioning tests after TPS upgrades and comparing them with commissioning baselines.
note: Section 9: 'This report recommends these tests be conducted annually or following TPS system upgrades'; plans 'compared to the baseline obtained during commissioning'. Dose calculation only. MPPG 5.a (2015) has the same text, and 5.b supersedes it.

claim: IAEA TRS-430 asks the user to compare plans calculated with the new and the previous software version after an update, and divides duties: the vendor supplies detailed information on software updates; the user implements, commissions and QAs upgrades.
note: Sections 10.3.4, 7.7.1(e) and 7.7.2(f); version records in 6.8.

claim: NCS Report 35 requires consistency testing between the current clinical TPS version and a new version, including contour volume calculation, and asks that the exact (sub)version and introduction date be documented.
note: Sections 6.1-6.3; Table 6.1 item 3. Section 6.2 also asks what workflow is needed for patients already in treatment preparation at release.

claim: Vandewinckele et al. recommend recommissioning after model updates (test phase for minor updates, training/validation phase for major ones) and periodic re-prediction of a commissioning reference set to verify consistency after software updates.
note: Fig. 2 caption; Implementation; Quality assurance, Routine model QA.

claim: The joint ESTRO-AAPM guideline recommends having procedures for updates and upgrades in place before clinical introduction.
note: Statement 17 (highly recommended) and section 'Model QA/updates and upgrades'.

claim: The ESTRO-AAPM guideline specifies which metrics or tests should validate a model update.
note: It requires a procedure and prefers automated validation and testing for repeated retraining, but defines no metrics or acceptance criteria for updates.

claim: The ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR and RSNA statement says that a manufacturer's new model version may require re-evaluation at the user site, because benefits cannot be assumed to generalize locally.
note: Section 7, 'Periodic monitoring of model performance'. Wording is 'may require', not 'must'.

claim: IAEA Human Health Series No. 50 (2026) asks the clinically qualified medical physicist to verify AI performance before and after updates, to lead a new round of acceptance and commissioning after model updates, and not to release a new version that fails ad hoc QC.
note: Sections 5.4.6.1, 5.6, 5.6.10 and 5.8.3. Read from a third-party copy whose colophon matches the IAEA record; check against the official PDF.

claim: The RCR guidance states that a retrained auto-contouring model should carry a new version number and be evaluated before clinical use, and warns that DICOM version information can be lost when data move between systems.
note: Section 6, Post-implementation monitoring (November 2024 guidance; endorsed by the IPEM RT-SIG).

claim: AAPM's CAD subcommittee recommended that sites compare CAD output before and after each upgrade on a fixed test set, that manufacturers tell sites what is expected to change, and noted that segmentation boundaries may change with each software version.
note: Sections II.A (R1, R4 note 3, R6), II.B.1, II.B.3, III.B, V.C.

claim: The FDA, Health Canada and MHRA guiding principles for PCCPs call for verification and validation of planned changes, characterization of the device before and after changes, and transparency to users.
note: Principles 1, 3 and 4 (October 2023).

claim: The paper's current sentence, that regulators invite manufacturers of AI-enabled device software to submit PCCPs describing how each planned update will be validated before it is implemented, is accurate.
note: The Modification Protocol covers data management, re-training, performance evaluation and update procedures. Note that a PCCP is optional and covers only planned modifications; other changes still need a new submission.

claim: The FDA PCCP guidance recommends that labeling state how users will be informed of implemented modifications (for example a version history) and reflect the current version(s) of the AI-DSF.
note: Sections V.C and VII.B(4) of the guidance issued 18 August 2025 (originally 4 December 2024).

claim: The FDA PCCP guidance asks manufacturers whether data from previous device use will be rerun on the updated model and whether clinically meaningful before/after differences will be communicated.
note: Appendix A, item 4.c.9; item 4.c.4 asks how version information is shown with device outputs. These are example questions in non-binding guidance, not requirements.

claim: Under the EU AI Act, a high-risk AI system that undergoes a substantial modification (a change not foreseen in the initial conformity assessment that affects compliance or the intended purpose) needs a new conformity assessment.
note: Art. 3(23) and Art. 43(4), first subparagraph. Applies also when the system 'continues to be used by the current deployer'.

claim: The EU AI Act treats any vendor update as a substantial modification unless it was pre-determined.
note: Only changes that affect compliance or the intended purpose are substantial modifications, and the pre-determined-change exemption in Art. 43(4) is worded for systems 'that continue to learn after being placed on the market'. MDCG 2025-6 Q30 repeats that scope. Commission guidelines (Art. 96(1)(c)) were not found.

claim: A deployer that makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system becomes its provider.
note: Art. 25(1)(b); Art. 25(2) amended in 2026 to detail what the initial provider must hand over.

claim: Deployers of high-risk AI systems must use them according to the instructions, monitor their operation and keep automatically generated logs for at least six months.

AI Act technical documentation must identify the system version and its relation to previous versions; instructions for use must cover pre-determined changes and maintenance including software updates.
note: Annex IV points 1(a), 1(c) and 2(f); Art. 13(3)(c) and (e).

claim: AI Act obligations for AI medical devices (Art. 6(1), Annex I) apply from 2 August 2027.
